newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Oil union shuts down Colombia's main pipelines.
newsitem.headline: Oil union shuts down Colombia's main pipelines.

text.p: Oil workers paralyzed Colombia's two main oil pipelines, frequent targets of leftist guerrilla attacks, on Wednesday as part of a 24-hour wildcat strike, the state oil company Ecopetrol said.

Operations were also halted in Ecopetrol's refineries in the oil production center of Barrancabermeja and the Caribbean port of Cartagena while white collar workers found their entry to company offices in Bogota barred by picket lines.

The oil workers' union, USO, ordered the stoppage to pressure the government to scrap plans to restructure Ecopetrol, which it fears may be a first step away from its eventual privatization, and to protest demands by British Petroleum to renegotiate an association contract with Ecopetrol.

"This is the first time pumping has been suspended along these pipelines as a result of union actions. We have not yet evaluated any lost production costs but we will be carrying out thorough checks to make sure no equipment has been damaged or sabotaged," an Ecopetrol spokesman said.

He said the USO strike had prevented more than 220,000 barrels of oil being pumped along the pipeline that runs from fields operated by U.S. multinational Occidental Petroleum in Cano Limon, northwest Colombia, to Covenas on the Atlantic coast.
That pipeline, opened 10 years ago, has been dynamited by leftist guerrillas more than 40 times this year alone, costing millions of dollars in damage and lost production.

The pumping of a further 150,000 barrels was suspended along the four-year-old Colombia pipeline, the other to be hit by the strike. It runs through the eastern plains to Covenas, serving foreign oil companies BP, Triton and Total.
USO leaders said an estimated 6,000 workers were taking part in the strike, scheduled to end at 6 a.m. local time (1100 GMT) Thursday.

"Today's action has been a success. It is the first time the union has managed to halt pumping operations along these pipelines. But so far we have had no response from the government," Gustavo Triana, the USO social security secretary, said.

The government has given no hint that it will cede to USO's demands. Energy and Mines Minister Rodrigo Villamizar appeared before Congress Wednesday and said the government was considering the possibility of revising BP's contract with Ecopetrol in the Piedemonte field, which it complains is unprofitable.
Talks between the union and the government are due to take place over the next two weeks. Triana said an indefinite general strike could be called if demands were not met.
Wednesday's wildcat strike followed similar action in Barrancabermeja last Friday in protest at the killing of a top union official by an unidentified gunman.
